source.title: Scaling Laws of Decoder-Only Models on the Multilingual Machine Translation Task
source.authors: Gaëtan Caillaut; M. Nakhle; Raheel Qader; Jing-Shu Liu; Jean-gabriel Barthelemy

record.file_problem: No major problem; the text includes flattened tables and figure-only results.
record.tranche_reason: Applies scaling-law measurements to decoder-only models trained from scratch for multilingual machine translation, a new task setting.
record.gate_note: The study measures test loss across model sizes and training data, fits scaling laws and compares predictions with larger runs, and tests architecture scaling and downstream translation metrics. Reported values used only to configure models are not treated as outcomes.
record.test_reason: Trains six decoder-only translation models from scratch (70M–6.9B). It fits power laws (Eq. 1 in N; Chinchilla form in N, D) to test loss and checks extrapolation from smaller fits to 6.9B. It also compares width and depth scaling and relates size to BLEU, COMET and CometKiwi. This is a new setting (supervised MT, target-only loss) with its own results on V2, V4, V5, V6 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that decoder-only MT models follow LLM-like scaling laws (Chinchilla form applies) and recommend LLM training recipes for MT. Fitted laws fail beyond an unknown model or data size and do not transfer across domains or directions. At fixed FLOP, more data is often preferable to larger models. Width and depth scaling give similar loss, with width more hardware-efficient.
record.recipe_differences: Uses decoder-only models trained from scratch on sentence-pair translation data, with target-only loss; tests parameter and data scaling using power-law and Chinchilla-form fits rather than general-language-model pretraining.
record.method_sensitivity: Fit subset and training-data distribution (domain and translation direction) change the fitted curves and predictive performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Packing sentence pairs without cross-sample masking makes <eos> act as a start-of-translation cue. Omitting it at inference drops BLEU (e.g. 410M 40.85 vs 46.82), enough that 410M without the prefix underperforms 160M with it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-format or packing artifacts can outweigh model-size gains in measured loss or quality.

record.problems: Only six model sizes are tested. Fits from smaller subsets do not reliably predict the largest model, and the paper cannot specify a reliable range for extrapolation. Several loss and architecture results are presented only in plots, with no uncertainty estimates reported.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted Table 4 scores for external LLM comparators because they are not part of this study's model-size scaling sweep. Omitted per-direction appendix metrics and step-by-step checkpoints; the main scaling findings and all six models' Table 4 metrics are retained.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss of general text language models; the study's loss is target-only translation loss.
Extrapolation over several orders of magnitude; the largest gap tested is about 7–11x in parameters, at a single data distribution.
Compute-optimal N and D as powers of compute; no exponent estimates, no comparison with the Kaplan or Hoffmann splits.
Shape at strictly fixed parameter count over a wide range; only two depth/width pairs around a 70M base, matched on FLOP.
Image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer.
Non-translation downstream tasks; no quantitative loss-to-metric fit or correlation coefficient.
Parameter-counting conventions, training schedule and optimizer choices not varied systematically. Learning rate changes at 1B are a confound, not a test.

missing.what: Chinchilla-fit projections: 70M with 4x data matches 410M; 610M with 2x data matches 6.9B; 160M with about 2x data matches 410M within 410M's FLOP
Larger models always converge faster and reach a given loss with less data (sample efficiency)
Width-scaled variants have higher throughput than depth-scaled ones (900 vs 760 and 725 vs 445 samples/s) at similar loss
Separate row for Chinchilla fit excluding 6.9B being 'very close' to the all-model curve

record.verdict_notes: Evidence is mostly figure-only with six model sizes and no uncertainty estimates. Max learning rate drops from 1e-3 to 1e-4 at 1B and above, which may confound the 6.9B deviation from the small-model fits. Eq. 1 uses 'trainable parameters' while the Chinchilla fit uses non-embedding N, an untested counting choice. Text–table conflicts: the Fig. 3 caption versus the text on the ≤1B subset fit; the CometKiwi financial peak (text says 610M, Table 4 shows 160M); Table 5 parameter counts versus its caption. V3 is given no verdict: the fixed-FLOP result is consistent with data-heavy allocation but estimates no compute exponents.

versions.untested_parts: The models are trained for machine translation from scratch, with loss calculated only on target translation tokens; the study does not test held-out pretraining loss for language modeling.
The study tests prediction of its largest model from smaller runs, but not prediction across several orders of magnitude.
It compares model and data choices at fixed FLOP budgets and fits a Chinchilla-form law, but does not estimate stable power exponents for optimal parameter and token counts as compute grows.
Tests selected width and depth changes from a 70M baseline, not a wide range of architecture details.
Tests multilingual, multidomain machine translation trained from scratch; does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Tests translation metrics against model size and test loss, not a broad set of downstream tasks.
Shows sensitivity to fit subsets and data distribution, but does not systematically compare parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, or fitting algorithms.
